How to Draw a Mandala: A Step-by-Step Guide for Beginners

By Super Mandala Lab · October 28, 2026

Drawing a mandala looks complicated, but it comes down to one idea: draw a shape, then repeat it evenly around a center. Once you set up a few guidelines, the symmetry does most of the work. This guide walks through drawing one by hand, then shows how to do the same thing in a few minutes online.

What you need

  • Plain paper or a sketchbook (smooth, heavier paper takes ink and markers better)
  • A pencil and a good eraser
  • A compass, or a few round objects to trace such as cups, lids and tape rolls
  • A ruler and a protractor
  • A fine-tip black pen for inking
  • Colored pencils, markers or paint, if you want to color it

Step 1: Mark the center

Lightly mark a dot in the middle of the page. Everything in the mandala grows out from this point, so take a moment to center it.

Step 2: Draw guide circles

With the compass point on the center, draw five or six light circles at different distances. They don't need to be evenly spaced. These circles become the rings where each layer of shapes sits.

Step 3: Divide the circle into slices

Use the protractor to divide the circle into equal slices and draw light lines from the center to the outer circle. Divide 360 by the number of slices you want: 8 slices means a line every 45 degrees, 12 slices every 30 degrees, and 16 slices every 22.5 degrees.

No protractor? Draw a vertical and a horizontal line through the center to get 4 slices, then split each slice in half by eye to get 8, and again to get 16.

Step 4: Start at the center

Draw a small circle or flower in the middle. Then, in the first ring, draw one simple shape, such as a petal, in one slice. Repeat that exact shape in every slice around the ring. Use the guide lines to keep each copy the same width and angle.

Step 5: Build outward one ring at a time

Move to the next guide circle and choose a different shape: teardrops, arches, dots, triangles or scallops. Repeating a shape around a ring is what makes it read as a mandala, and changing shapes from ring to ring keeps it interesting.

Two tricks make designs look richer:

  • Offset by half a slice. Place the shapes in one ring between the shapes of the ring inside it, like bricks.
  • Echo a shape. Draw a smaller copy inside a petal or teardrop to add detail without new ideas.

Step 6: Close it with a border

Finish with an outer ring: a plain circle, a scalloped edge, or a band of small dots. A border makes the design feel complete.

Step 7: Ink it and erase the guides

Go over the lines you want to keep with the fine-tip pen. Let the ink dry fully, then erase the pencil guidelines.

Step 8: Color it

Color one ring at a time and repeat the same color in every slice of that ring. Alternating light and dark rings gives a mandala depth. If you want a calmer look, pick three or four colors and stick to them.

Tips for beginners

  • Start with 8 slices. Even numbers are easier because you can fold or halve them. Odd numbers like 5 or 7 look great but are harder to measure.
  • Keep shapes simple. A circle, a petal and a triangle repeated well look better than complicated shapes repeated unevenly.
  • Work lightly in pencil. You'll erase a lot, and that's normal.
  • Turn the paper. Rotating the page so each slice is in front of you makes repeats more even.
